articles.title: South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
articles.summary: Lee Jae Myung offers chance to end the conflict, which has been frozen since an armistice in 1953.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said talks could yield "peaceful coexistence" By Aleks Phillips 
- Published 15 August 2026 
South Korea's president has proposed talks with its northern neighbour on officially ending the war between the two that is technically still active. 
Lee Jae Myung suggested a "multi-layered security system" to avoid flare-ups along the countries' de-facto border, known as the demilitarised zone (DMZ), and offered to discuss practical ways of halting Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions. 
North Korea has continually tested ballistic missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads, which has been perceived in Seoul and nearby Japan as an attempt to intimidate and project power. 
The conflict between the two occupants of the Korean peninsula has been effectively frozen since an armistice was signed in 1953. 
They did not sign a peace treaty and therefore have remained technically still at war ever since. 
There have been clashes and tensions along the DMZ in the decades since, along with accusations from both sides of provocations, including dropping balloons carrying rubbish and propaganda . 
Lee, who became South Korean president last year after his predecessor Yoon Suk Yeol was impeached for attempting to declare martial law, has sought to thaw relations with North Korea and its ally China, which had soured under Yoon. 
"Let us put down our intentions to threaten each other and begin discussions to end the long-running war as the directly involved parties," he told a ceremony marking Liberation Day, which commemorates the peninsula's liberation from Japanese rule. 
Lee expressed hope that the two nations "will sit face-to-face for peaceful coexistence and mutual growth", adding this could serve as a forum for discussing "effective ways to halt the advancement of the North's nuclear capabilities". 
North Korea has yet to react to Lee's offer. The authoritarian regime's state news agency carried news of Kim marking the country's own Liberation Day commemorations with a wreath-laying and guard of honour. 
Pyongyang has previously rebuffed Lee's offers of engagement, criticising a deal for the US to build South Korea a fleet of nuclear-powered submarines and denouncing joint drills between the two allies. 
In January 2024, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced that unification with the South was no longer possible. 
Kim said that the constitution should be amended to educate North Koreans that South Korea was a "primary foe and invariable principal enemy". 
In a speech at the time, he added that if a war were to break out on the Korean peninsula, the North should aim towards "occupying", "recapturing" and "incorporating" the South into its territory. 
North Korea declared itself a nuclear power in 2022 and vowed never to relinquish its weapons, of which it is estimated , external to possess dozens. 
Lee has previously said Pyongyang was producing 15 to 20 more warheads annually, telling the BBC last year he would back a deal between US President Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un to freeze production. 
Trump is the only Western leader to have met Kim, which happened during the US president's first term. 
Though he has turned his attention to other regions since returning to the White House, Trump said last August that he hoped to meet Kim again when "appropriate". 
In a sign of continued sabre-rattling, North Korea fired a ballistic missile into the sea on Tuesday - the 11th suspected test so far this year - just days before a scheduled US-South Korean joint military exercise.

articles.title: 'Unprecedented' rain in Japan kills eight people
articles.summary: The storm cut power to more than 20,000 households and left 7,000 people stranded at Tokyo's Narita airport.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Record rainfall causes flooding in Japan’s Chiba region By Kelly Ng   and   Kurumi Mori ,  Tokyo correspondent 
- Published 14 August 2026 
At least eight people have died as record rainfall pummelled eastern Japan and left thousands stranded at Tokyo's Narita Airport. 
The rains, which authorities have described as "unprecedented", cut power to more than 20,000 households in Chiba prefecture. 
Local authorities issued a level five emergency warning, its highest alert, on Thursday. This was downgraded to a level four by Friday morning, but they continue to warn of landslide and flooding risks. 
The deluge comes after a series of storms swept through Japan and neighbouring countries this week, in what meteorologists forecast to be an unusually active typhoon season. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Cars were left abandoned in the streets of Oamishirasato, in Chiba 
Japan's Meteorological Agency said the most recent deluge was brought by warm, humid air flowing into the country's east that combined with cold air above to make atmospheric conditions extremely unstable. 
The rains are expected to last through late on Friday. 
"This case was an extremely unusual situation, even by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday morning. 
"I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this." 
Chiba, which sits right next to Tokyo, has logged more than 100mm of rain per hour since Thursday afternoon, authorities say. 
This is about three times the average rainfall in August, and the highest volume of precipitation ever recorded in the country. 
Authorities would prioritise saving lives and persist with rescue efforts, Kumagai added. 
At least eight people have died, according to reports from public broadcaster NHK, Kyodo news agency and Asahi newspaper. 
Among those killed was a woman who died inside her car submerged on a flooded road, authorities said. Two others collapsed along the streets and later died. 
The Japan Meteorological Agency earlier described the situation as an "unprecedented level of heavy rain". 
Several rail services remain suspended on Friday morning while some major highways are also shut. 
More than 100,000 households have been asked to evacuate on Thursday after the rain triggered landslides and power outages. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Thousands were stranded overnight at Narita as the storm disrupted transportation to and from the airport 
All flights were scheduled to operate normally on Friday, a spokesperson from Narita airport said. Flag carrier Japan Airlines said some of its flights may be delayed but that it does not expect any cancellations. 
Passengers were stranded at metro stations, while around 1,800 people spent the night at the Chiba Prefectural Government building. 
A woman in Chiba's Ichikawa city told NHK the rain "happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise". 
"The power is out so I'm worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days," she said. 
Meanwhile in the Philippines, authorities have again shut schools and government offices are again shut in most of the country's north, citing the threat of floods. 
Earlier this week, Japan, the Philippines and China were hit by back-to-back storms – Dolphin, Chan-Hom and Peilou – churning across the region at the same time. 
Dolphin brought heavy rain to Japan's Okinawa island, cutting power to tens of thousands of buildings, toppling trees and cancelling flights. 
Over the weekend, Chinese authorities evacuated more than a million people from their homes as Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, made landfall in the country's east.

articles.title: Delhi's unusual challenge: Keeping monkeys and pigeons away from top badminton event
articles.summary: After wildlife intrusions made headlines at an earlier tournament, organisers are taking extra measures for the badminton world championships.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The BWF World Championships will begin in Delhi on Monday By Nikita Yadav BBC News, Delhi 
- Published 14 August 2026 
Sports authorities in India are taking extra measures to keep monkeys and pigeons away from a major international badminton tournament in Delhi after wildlife intrusions overshadowed another competition earlier this year. 
In January, when India hosted the India Open badminton tournament, organisers had hoped the headlines would be about tense matches, some of the world's best players and the excitement of hosting a major tournament in the capital. 
Instead, the event became a talking point for very different reasons. There were complaints about air pollution, matches were halted , external because of pigeon droppings on the court and a monkey was spotted inside the stadium. 
Now, as Delhi prepares to host the BWF World Championships from Monday, organisers are taking steps to ensure the focus remains on the sport. 
The tournament - one of the biggest events in the badminton calendar - will be held at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium from 17 to 23 August. 
Officials told the BBC that wooden doors across the stadium have been replaced with double-door systems that lock automatically. High-grade nets have also been installed over openings where birds or animals could potentially enter. 
"We have also used a non-toxic gel in places and on handles where the pigeons could have landed as a secondary measure," said Sanjay Mishra, general secretary of the Badminton Association of India. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Langur posters were put up across Delhi during the G20 summit in 2023 to scare away monkeys 
Other possible entry points, including gaps in the roof and exhaust vents, have also been sealed or repaired, he added. 
The stadium has also undergone an overhaul to improve the look and feel of the arena. The Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium was built for the 1982 Asian Games and later renovated ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games. 
"Structural upgrades have been carried out at the three major arenas in the stadium," Ambar Pratap Singh, executive director of Sports Authority of India, said in a video posted on social media. 
The lighting has also been fixed after players complained during the India Open about shadows appearing on the court, he added. 
But it is the efforts to keep monkeys away from the venue that have attracted the most attention ahead of the tournament. 
A video showing a man apparently mimicking the call of a langur - large, long-tailed monkeys found across much of South Asia - went viral on social media in India earlier this week. 
Langur's calls have traditionally been used to scare away smaller rhesus macaques, which are common in the city. 
Several Indian and international news outlets reported that men who mimic langurs had been hired to keep away other monkeys. 
Even two-time badminton Olympic medallist PV Sindhu wrote on X: "Our solutions may be uniquely Indian, but so are our warmth, our spirit and our hospitality." 
But senior official Mishra told the BBC that the association had not specifically employed anyone as part of measures for the championships. 
He said that because the stadium covers a large area, a person who could imitate langur calls was briefly present in the northern block. 
The use of langurs to scare away rhesus macaques is not new in India, especially Delhi. During the 2010 Commonwealth Games , authorities used black-faced langurs at some venues to scare away smaller rhesus macaques. 
In 2023, when India hosted the G20 summit, authorities put up life-size cutouts of langurs across the capital to scare monkeys away. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
India Open 2026 made more headlines for poor air quality and animal intrusions than the matches 
But monkeys were only one of the problems at the January games. 
During the tournament, a men's singles match between Singapore's Loh Kean Yew and India's HS Prannoy was stopped twice after pigeon droppings fell onto the court. 
Then, there was also bad air. 
Between October and January, air pollution in northern India - especially capital Delhi - reaches hazardous levels. It happened this year as well and players complained about it. 
Singapore's Loh said he struggled to breathe and wore a mask outside his hotel room, while Denmark's Mia Blichfeldt described the conditions as "unhealthy". 
For India, the incidents were embarrassing as it seeks to establish itself as a major host of international sporting events. The country is set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has also bid for the 2036 Olympics. 
The badminton world championships are an opportunity for India to show that it can stage a major global sporting event and keep attention focused on the competition. 
This year's tournament will feature the reigning men's and women's world champions - China's Shi Yuqi and Japan's Akane Yamaguchi, respectively. 
India will be hoping for a strong performance on home soil, with Sindhu leading its challenge in the women's singles. 
For the organisers, there is therefore plenty at stake. They will want the biggest stories from Delhi over the next week to be about the players, the matches and badminton, rather than the wildlife.

articles.title: BTS star V reveals hearing loss battle during livestream
articles.summary: The K-pop star says he has suffered hearing issues for over two years before revealing it publicly this week.
articles.full_text:
Image source, MLB Photos via Getty Images Image caption, 
BTS member V says he has been dealing with hearing issues for more than two years By Koh Ewe 
- Published 13 August 2026 
V, a member of pop sensation BTS, says he has been receiving treatment for hearing loss in one ear, an announcement that comes midway through the band's highly-anticipated world tour. 
In a livestream on Wednesday, the 30-year-old said that he has dealt with the problem for about two and a half years. This was the first time he was revealing it to the band's fans, he said. 
"If the hearing in my left ear is at 100, it's only about 30 in my right," said V, whose real name is Kim Tae-hyung. 
The band is currently on its first world tour in years, marking the reunion of all seven members since they went on a hiatus for mandatory military service. 
During the livestream, V said his hearing became worse when he was serving in the military. 
But he said he did not take it seriously at first, believing it to be "a matter of mental strength". 
He added he was now taking medication and going to hospital regularly. 
With rare exceptions, all able-bodied men are required to serve 18 months of military service in South Korea. 
This included BTS members, who were at the height of their fame in 2022 when they started taking career breaks to enlist in the military. 
V joined the military in 2023 and was discharged in June 2025. 
The Arirang World Tour, which kicked off in April in South Korea, marked the highly-anticipated reunion of the band's seven members. 
The livestream on Wednesday came after the band wrapped its concerts in Baltimore, Maryland. 
V was joined by his bandmate Jungkook, who talked about a shin injury he has been dealing with during the tour, saying he was "on the verge of developing a stress fracture". 
Jungkook added that he would have to manage his injury well in order to keep performing. 
In the coming months, the concert tour will take BTS to cities around the world, including Los Angeles, Buenos Aires, Bangkok, Sydney and Hong Kong.

articles.title: South Korea's Incheon airport becomes world's busiest for global traffic
articles.summary: The airport said diversions caused by the Middle East conflict helped boost its traffic, while Heathrow was ranked second.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Incheon International Airport is the main gateway to South Korea By Kelly Ng 
- Published 13 August 2026 
South Korea's Incheon has become the world's busiest airport by international passenger traffic for the first time, new figures show. 
Incheon International Airport, the main gateway to South Korea, served 38.4 million international passengers for the first six months of this year, according to preliminary data from the Airports Council International. 
London Heathrow Airport ranked second with 37.79 million passengers, followed by Singapore's Changi Airport with 34.53 million. 
Incheon's airport attributed its rise partly to the diversion of passengers from aviation hubs in the Middle East because of the conflict between the US and Iran. 
Dubai International Airport, which ranked second both in 2024 and 2025 based on full-year statistics, is expected to fall outside the top five this time. 
London's Heathrow airport ranked fifth in 2024 and seventh in 2025, while Incheon ranked 12th and 13th, respectively. 
Some passengers who previously transited through Dubai on the way to Europe are now travelling via Incheon, the airport corporation said, fuelling an 18% rise in transfer passengers from the same period last year. 
The number of transfer passengers whose final destinations were in Europe rose 63.2% to 210,000, it added. 
The corporation said the expansion of infrastructure also enabled the airport to manage a larger traffic load. Incheon, which opened in 2001, serves 158 international destinations. 
In comparison, Hong Kong's International Airport serves 139 destinations, Shanghai's Pudong serves 92 while Tokyo's Narita serves 86. 
"We're grateful for the [South Korean] government's support, the public's encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport in making Incheon the world's No. 1 airport," said the Incheon airport corporation's acting president Kim Beom-ho. 
Kim added the corporation planned to strengthen competitiveness by focusing on passenger convenience.

articles.title: Japan PM says Putin's visit to disputed islands 'absolutely unacceptable'
articles.summary: It was the first time the Russian leader had visited the Kuril islands, according to state media.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Russia's President Vladimir Putin tastes caviar as he visits Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu By Koh Ewe   and   Kurumi Mori ,  Tokyo correspondent 
- Published 13 August 2026 
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has criticised Vladimir Putin's first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril islands on Thursday as "absolutely unacceptable". 
Russian state media reported that Putin visited Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, one of four islands in the Kuril chain that are claimed by Russia and Japan. 
Putin's trip "has worsened Japanese sentiment towards Russia," Takaichi told reporters, maintaining the island chain was "a unique territory of [Japan] historically and under international law". 
The countries have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. 
The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. Four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. 
They are administered by Russia. At the end of World War Two, the Soviet Union annexed the island chain and deported around 17,000 Japanese residents. 
During his visit, Putin sampled fish roe and spoke to island locals, Russian state media reported. 
Speaking from the prime minister's office on Thursday, Takaichi said his trip "wounds the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories". 
"I hope that the Russian side will take the gravity of this matter very seriously," she said. 
Earlier that day, Japan's foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said the islands were "inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit". 
Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. 
Japan has protested against previous visits by Russian officials to the disputed islands, including Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his predecessor Dmitry Medvedev. 
The Kuril islands are a strategic area for Russia, which has beefed up its military presence on the islands over the past decade. The island of Iturup is used as its primary military air base in the region. 
Last month, Chinese and Russian naval warships sailed through a strait in the Kuril islands during a joint patrol. 
Russia also holds regular military drills near the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan.

articles.title: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?
articles.summary: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, many are asking whether the West has any bargaining chips left
articles.full_text:
By Lyse Doucet Chief international correspondent ,  Reporting from Kabul 
In a whitewashed basement in a village south of Kabul, a dozen young women bustle about, stirring cauldrons of bubbling cherries and plums, and sticking labels on glass jam jars. Ventures like this are one of the rare spaces where women are still able to gain skills and employment in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. 
It is run by Najia, a 47-year-old Afghan entrepreneur and mother of nine children who was married at the age of 14. 
If the authorities hadn't barred girls and young women from secondary schools and universities, many of the women in this workshop, including Naija's daughters, would be studying for a different kind of future. 
Image caption, 
Jam-making workshops are one of vanishingly few ways women can still learn and make money 
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering. 
"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope." 
Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change? 
The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response. 
Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working. 
Engage, not isolate 
Few voices call for absolute isolation, not when the United Nations warns that 22 million Afghans – nearly half the of the population – rely on some form of foreign assistance to help them survive. 
The country has been battered by multiple shocks: an agonising economic crisis; devastating natural disasters; clashes with neighbouring Pakistan, and the influx of millions of Afghans deported from countries near and far into this impoverished land. 
And there's no avoiding it – the Taliban are in charge now. 
In the years since their fighters swept into Kabul on 15 August 2021, they've grown in confidence and consolidated control despite intermittent attacks by armed opposition groups based abroad, as well as Islamic State fighters. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The Taliban took Kabul in a lightning offensive 
The Taliban are collecting tax revenues and signing deals in mining, energy and more with Beijing, Moscow, Abu Dhabi, and Tashkent, along with other neighbours. 
But they're still strangled by international sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights. Russia is the only country to formally recognise their rule, and they haven't been allowed to take up what they see as their rightful seat at the UN in New York. 
But formal diplomatic recognition is no longer the focal point. 
"The West is losing the argument over recognition," says a former senior UN official who requested anonymity because they continue to work in Afghanistan. They point to the growing number of countries which have conferred de facto recognition by clinching deals, accrediting diplomats, operating embassies, and more. 
"There's no doubt the Taliban would like to be recognised at the UN but it's no longer as potent a bargaining chip as it was at the beginning," they assess. 
Behind the soaring blast walls of the foreign ministry in Kabul, in the sprawling compound of manicured lawns and graceful historic buildings, Taliban diplomats keep adding names and flags to the growing collection of Afghan embassies worldwide which are now under their control, rather than the last holdouts of the government they ousted. The current tally is more than 40. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Natural disasters and poverty have caused further problems 
"We need to come closer diplomatically rather than talking from a distance if we want to make progress in our relationship," says Zabihullah Mujahid, the main Taliban spokesman. 
We meet in Kandahar in southern Afghanistan, the real seat of power. This is where the Taliban's reclusive emir, Hibatullah Akhundzada, has been steadily building his political and military base and issuing hundreds of edicts, many of them focused on erasing women and girls from public life – what he portrays as an Islamic obligation to protect them. 
This five-year mark is widely seen as an inflection point. 
"An unstable and potentially dangerous equilibrium," is how the situation was described in closed-door remarks by a senior UN official at a recent international gathering. 
And, yet, Afghanistan has fallen far under the world's radar. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East absorb international attention, and Europe's burning issue is how to stop so many Afghans fleeing towards their shores. It's a startling reversal. 
"It's extraordinary given the scale of Western effort from 2001-2021 how ignored Afghanistan is now," remarks a Western diplomat who recently served as an envoy to the country. They did not want to be named because they're still in the diplomatic service. 
Image source, BBC/Prem Boominathan Image caption, 
Zabihullah Mujahid says closer diplomacy will help talks 
"The real diplomatic gap is the US," they added, in reference to the current US administration's decision to eliminate their special envoy position and dismantle many agencies, including the US Agency for International Development (USAID), which once led the world's approach on almost every Afghan issue. 
Even within Taliban ranks, especially among those known to differ with some of the strictest edicts handed down by their emir, there is frustration that the world doesn't seem willing or able to forge a different kind of relationship. 
"We want to be part of the international community," emphasises Mullah Abdul Salam Zaeef, a founding member of the Taliban who now runs a madrasa for boys and girls on the outskirts of Kabul. Unlike mainstream schools, madrasas take girls of all ages and some, especially those run privately, are teaching more than religious classes. 
"Just putting pressure won't work," he tells us. He takes the long view of Afghanistan's history of resisting foreign invaders. "We didn't surrender to the Russians, to the Americans, so why would the Taliban surrender now?" 
Open dialogue 
UN officials believe their presence in Afghanistan makes a difference, however limited. They point to progress on issues such as the treatment of prisoners, their detailed discussions on the harsh implementation of the morality code known as the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, as well as efforts to improve humanitarian access. 
"Engagement is slow, progress is incremental, and reversals are frequent," is the UN's sober summary of the past five years of on-off dialogue. 
But it still insists it needs to stay the course. 
"A stalled process is better than no process," emphasises Georgette Gagnon, a deputy special representative of the secretary-general for Afghanistan, who is now the acting head of the UN mission in Kabul. 
The UN has been criticised for not pushing back enough against the Taliban, including for holding forums such as the so-called Doha Process , in which a Taliban delegation travelled to the Qatari capital in 2024 to discuss a range of issues, on condition that no Afghan women's representatives were at the table. UN officials insist all issues were discussed, and that subsequent meetings included their participation. 
A new process called Mosaic approaches negotiations in a more structured format, on six core issues. On one side there are human rights including women's rights, inclusive governance, and counterterrorism. On the other, there are Taliban demands – sanctions relief, unfreezing assets, diplomatic representation. 
"Confidence and reciprocity are beginning to take shape to open the door to engagement on the most difficult issues," says Gagnon whom we meet inside the UN's vast, heavily fortified compound. She calls them "small steps on the long road". 
She insists it has to be done through a collective effort, not only through discussions by individual governments. "Pressure has not worked so far, threats have not worked; our best chance lies in consistent and common messaging and action." 
For some sceptics, even inside the UN, there's worry that the Mosaic approach isn't going to work either. 
But just keeping the lights on, preventing a slide into isolation, and continuing protection work with vulnerable communities, especially women, is seen as essential. 
Talk quietly 
In dusty provincial capitals and farmers' fields, where international and Afghan aid agencies wrestle with ways to work on the ground, the conversations continue day in day out. 
It's there that edicts handed down by the reclusive emir are translated into what are known as workarounds. These workarounds can mean women are able to work in some agency sectors from home, or in different rooms, on different floors, or even in different buildings to men. 
"Everything in Afghanistan is relationships, and day-to-day that can help make things easier," says Chris Kinder, the chairman of Afghanaid, a British charity which has been working in Afghanistan for more than 40 years. He emphasises that most of these conversations on access and implementation are conducted by experienced Afghan staff. 
My own visits to provincial cities and towns in recent years have underscored how some local Taliban officials try to find pragmatic solutions. But others remain deeply suspicious of any foreign assistance. 
Local agreements were described by another charity as "verbal and fragile". 
Kinder rejects criticism that aid agencies have had to compromise on principles to keep their projects in place. 
"The Taliban have their red lines and we, and our donors, have ours. We discuss approaches so both sides understand where they are coming from." 
Here too, many aid officials call for a more unified approach. 
Talk tougher 
"We need to keep talking, but now we need to set conditions," is the view of Najia the jam maker. It's a stance also taken by women activists in the diaspora and human rights groups who say dialogue has been a one-way street, with the Taliban not offering any significant changes in return. 
They insist discussion should not go beyond aid issues until they do. 
A recent flashpoint was the decision by EU officials in June to host a Taliban foreign ministry delegation in Brussels for the first time since the Taliban returned to power. Representatives of 15 member states joined this one-day meeting to discuss processes to send back Afghan nationals who had no legal right to remain in the EU. 
The EU called them "technical-level" talks. The Taliban saw them differently. A spokesperson described the agenda as including possible consular presence in Europe and the "need for trust-building measures". 
"The diplomatic community is well aware that there are already existing channels through which technical issues can be discussed with the Taliban," says Rina Amiri, an Afghan-born former American diplomat who served as the US special envoy for Afghan women, girls and human rights from 2022 to 2025 and also grappled with the terms under which to meet the Taliban. 
"Meeting in Brussels was clearly a decision that was about politics, not logistics," she says. 
The critics call it "creeping normalisation". 
Will it work? 
"After these last five years I spent in Afghanistan, what do I have to show?" asks Mahbouba Seraj, an Afghan activist who runs a shelter, when we visit her in Kabul. When the Taliban took over in 2021, Seraj made headlines when she announced that she would stay in her country to fight for women's rights. 
Seraj, 78, now says she's preparing to leave. 
Her last shelter, which provided a life-saving refuge for more than 30 Afghan women fleeing domestic abuse, was shut down in December. Her repeated appeals to Taliban leaders to re-open classrooms for women and girls have been ignored. 
"These small windows that the world sees, the little openings here and there including secret schools for girls, are just meant to fool everybody," she laments with visible sadness. 
But Seraj calls on the international community to keep talking. 
"They have to talk, but they have to make sure that when they sit down and talk, it's not just a lot of people just filling the air." 
Image caption, 
Activists say women and girls have been forgotten 
There are others who say the same. 
"Only more capable diplomacy through quiet and confidential engagement can deliver the change," says a former Afghan official who's been involved in discreet discussions with Taliban officials. He hopes whoever is chosen as the new UN Secretary General and takes office at the start of next year will engage more effectively. 
But, in the end, it's not the international community which is in the driving seat of any change. 
"I don't think the answer is the world finding the right language to talk to the Taliban," says a Western analyst who's long been involved in Afghanistan and like others interviewed for this article asked to remain anonymous. "Five years on, it's very clear that real change can only come from within." 
Some senior Taliban officials have occasionally spoken out about the emir's harshest orders, in particular the closure of girls' schools, and there've been rare instances when some were able to find ways to roll back his rules. One such case was last year's nation-wide internet shutdown which paralysed daily life and was later reversed.

articles.title: 'I lost $14,000 in a month': Investors hit by Korean stock market's wild swings
articles.summary: Some traders are reeling from heavy losses after a brutal correction in South Korea's stock market.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Kim Yongjoon Image caption, 
Yongjoon Kim, pictured with his partner, planned to use his investments to fund a new home as they are getting married later this year By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 13 August 2026 
Bank worker Yongjoon Kim lost 20 million Korean won ($14,000; £10,500) on the South Korean stock market last month. 
Kim's money was meant to help buy a home, as he is getting married later this year. 
Instead the value of his tech investments slumped by around 25% in July. 
"It's going to sting and I'm going to have to work really hard to make up for this," Kim says. "But for others who have taken more risk, they're going to feel the pain." 
Many of his friends are worse off, and now in a "desperate" situation after "going all in" with their savings, he says. 
While plenty of investors are piling into technology stocks , sharp market swings mean the bets don't always pay off, with prices often moving on every major headline. 
Nowhere is that instability more pronounced than in South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi, widely regarded as the world's most volatile stock index. 
A global frenzy around artificial intelligence has driven wild swings in the value of the country's biggest chipmakers. 
The Kospi faced "one of the sharpest corrections" in its history between June and August, comparable to the drops seen during Covid-19 and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, says Wee Khoon Chong from financial services company BNY. 
The index more than doubled its value since the start of the year to rise above 9,000 points in mid-June, before plunging to 5,500 within a few weeks. It has now recovered some ground to about 6,800 points. 
A key reason for the sell-off in recent weeks has been concerns over the huge amounts of money being spent on AI, Chong adds. 
The slump has had a big impact on many of the country's personal investors who bought tech stocks over the past year. 
For Woongsa Kim, a look at his shares trading app is a painful reminder of what he had made then lost by investing in the South Korean stock market. 
At the start of the year, he used about half of a bonus from work to buy shares in tech giant SK Hynix. 
The stock quadrupled in value before most of those gains were wiped out, leaving his investment, now worth about 300 million won, at roughly half the value of its peak. 
"Thinking about it just brings tears to my eyes," Kim told the BBC. 
Image source, Woongsa Kim Image caption, 
Woongsa Kim put half of a bonus into SK Hynix shares 
The sell-off came after tech shares had soared for months, "generating the extreme euphoria" that has moved some personal investors to take out loans to invest, says investment analyst Tobias Reger. 
It has been most acutely felt by people who used leverage - a form of borrowing in the financial markets. 
Leveraging lets an investor control a larger number of stocks than their own cash would otherwise allow, which delivers a bigger profit if the shares rise. 
However, if the stocks fall past an agreed level it can trigger what is known as a margin call - when a broker demands payment of the debt. 
By the end of July an estimated 1.2 million South Korean personal investor accounts had faced margin calls, equivalent to about one in every 30 working-age adults in the country. 
Leveraged trading is a growing trend among personal investors that has also picked up in markets like Taiwan and the US, says Frank Benzimra, the head of Asia equity strategy at financial services group Societe Generale. 
That has raised the risks around AI-related stocks, he adds. 
'Gut-wrenching' slump 
After his US-listed Nvidia shares soared by more than 1,000%, Chanyong Park, who works in marketing, says he put most of the profits into SK Hynix shares. But that bet went sour as their value has fallen by around $10,000. 
"This was money I'd invested to save before planning to leave my job around October to start my own business. But now I'm seriously wondering whether I'll have enough." 
Park plans to hold on to his SK Hynix shares in hopes of a rebound, although recent swings have made him hesitant to invest more. 
"It doesn't always feel like movements are driven by rational reasons - sometimes it still feels a lot like gambling," he says. 
Another investor Youngji Park says he went "all in", putting the majority of his available cash into Samsung shares that peaked at a total value of 45 million Korean won. 
But his investment has suffered a "gut-wrenching" slump, Park says.

He too plans to keep hold of his shares in the hope that they will rise again. 
"I feel like a fool for trusting the Korean stock market," he says. "It's a long-term game now. I'll just have to wait it out." 
College student Soomin Yi says she pooled money with a friend to invest in SK Hynix after experiencing "fomo" (fear of missing out). 
Image source, Soomin Yi Image caption, 
Soomin Yi says she did not study investing seriously before buying shares 
But she now wishes she had sold her shares in the company when they peaked at three million won each in June, instead of buying into speculation that they would rise to five million won. 
"We didn't really have anyone around us who is experienced in investing, and we did not study investing seriously before buying the stock," Yi says. 
What this means for the rest of the world 
The huge swings in Korean shares are also raising concerns about some other markets around the world. 
Tech-heavy indexes like Japan's Nikkei 225 seem to be moving in tandem with the Kospi's wild swings, Societe Generale's Benzimra says. 
But the majority of the world's stock markets are unlikely to see that level of violent moves as they include a wider mix of companies, he adds. 
"I don't think we can see the same kind of volatility in large diversified markets such as the [Tokyo Stock Price Index] or the US equity markets," Benzimra says. 
And traders who diversified their portfolios say it has helped cushion the blow from the stock market rout. 
"I think this whole episode is a warning to Korean investors, especially young investors, not to put everything in one basket and hope for the best," says Yongjoon Kim, who also has shares in overseas markets. 
He adds that he should have taken a more cautious approach to investing in tech stocks. 
His fiancée, Gaeon Lee, is optimistic that the market will recover despite losing part of the savings they had set aside for a new home. 
But she worries about Kim, saying the constant need to monitor their investments has taken a toll on him. 
"Seeing our home savings take a hit in the stock market was definitely a wake-up call," she says.

A fake website and a deluge of CVs: the Australian firm embroiled in an FBI probe into alleged Chinese espionage
Exclusive: Fake consultancy impersonating Brisbane firm online is one of 13 websites seized by the US Department of Justice

When the first emails arrived, they were easily dismissed as spam. But as strangers continued to boast about their defence and security credentials, they became impossible to ignore. 
From mid-2025, a small Australian consultancy firm called Horizzen started receiving emails and strange calls from people applying for vague jobs in the United States. 
It would have been an ambitious global expansion for the Brisbane-based firm, which only had a few domestic clients. Except, it wasn’t hiring. A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he? 
Read more 
Without its knowledge, a fake consultancy firm impersonating Horizzen had been launched online. It claimed to be an “architect of influence” and was overseeing a recruitment blitz for experts in defence, trade and politics. 
“It was using our company name, business address, phone number and content, but with a different design,” a Horizzen spokesperson said. 
“At first, I dismissed it as a cheap knock-off.” 
Some determined jobseekers, eager to impress, also sent their detailed CVs and cover letters to Horizzen’s Australian email address. They had been deceived into thinking they were the same organisation. 
In June – one year after the emails first arrived – Horizzen realised the scale of deception. 
The website falsely assuming its identity had been seized by the US Department of Justice, as part of an ongoing multi-agency investigation into alleged Chinese espionage. 
View image in fullscreen 
A screenshot from thehorizzen.com, which has been seized by the FBI as part of an ongoing investigation. 
The company had been drawn into what western intelligence agencies allege is a systematic campaign by Chinese spies to recruit and pressure people into revealing valuable secrets. 
Websites used to ‘trick, recruit, coerce’
In early June, Australia’s domestic intelligence agency joined counterparts in the UK, US, Canada and New Zealand to issue a rare public warning . They were convinced that Chinese spies were running fake consultancy firms and posing as recruiters on platforms such as LinkedIn. 
The intelligence services alleged that successful job applicants were tested for their knowledge of key issues, and then paid for reports. Eventually, the fake firms would push for “more privileged information” and switch to encrypted messaging services. 
“Chinese intelligence officers pose as online HR recruiters or consultants who represent fake, but often legitimate looking ‘cover companies’ and claim to be located in countries outside China ,” the joint Five Eyes statement said. 
Within 24 hours of that warning, the FBI obtained a warrant to seize the website impersonating Horizzen. It also shut down another 12 websites accused of targeting US citizens who have valuable knowledge. 
One allegedly belonged to a fake consultancy firm that was pretending to be based in Western Australia, a US court heard. Job adverts for the company were allegedly posted by someone based in Thailand. A LinkedIn profile for the consultancy firm remains online today, but claims its office is in Melbourne. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email 
In an affidavit provided to the court, a senior FBI officer alleged all 13 seized websites were created to “recruit individuals in the United States to obtain sensitive and possibly classified information in exchange for monetary payments” on China’s behalf. 
The FBI agent told the court that the websites used a mixture of aliases, stolen identities and AI-generated photographs to deceive applicants. 
According to the FBI, the consultancy firm pretending to be Horizzen told recruits they would “establish a formal relationship” with another consultancy firm, called Catalyst Global Solutions (CGS), whose website was also seized by the FBI. 
CGS’s website and job adverts claimed it was “among DC’s top firms”, despite having a listed address in Lahore, Pakistan. 
View image in fullscreen 
The Asio director general, Mike Burgess. The Australian security agency has previously warned Chinese spies are targeting people on LinkedIn. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images 
And, according to the FBI, CGS used an Australian job website to recruit analysts and consultants who specialised in “international relations” and “geo-politics”. 
In at least one case, it is accused of directly seeking an expert in the Indo-Pacific region. 
It is unknown whether they succeeded. 
When the 13 websites were seized, Roman Rozhavsky, the FBI’s assistant director responsible for counter-intelligence, alleged they “illustrate the lengths the Chinese government’s intelligence services will go to as they try to use AI-generated content to trick, recruit, or coerce”. 
That claim has been flatly rejected by the Chinese embassy in Canberra. 
An embassy spokesperson told Guardian Australia: “The US accusation has no factual basis and is purely smears and denigration. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
“China firmly opposes this.” 
‘Shock and disbelief’
In Brisbane, confirmation of the FBI’s investigation left the small team at Horizzen stunned. 
“My first reaction was shock and disbelief,” the company spokesperson said. 
“What is the reputational damage to the company and other people who may have been misled?” 
Horizzen believes its identity was deliberately copied by the fake consultancy firm to make it appear authentic, trusted and long-established. 
“I cannot say who created it or what they intended, but the extent of the copied information makes coincidence very difficult to accept,” a spokesperson said. 
“It clearly shows that identity theft can happen to any legitimate businesses.” 
View image in fullscreen 
‘What looks like ordinary spam may be connected to something far more sinister’ … Companies are urged not to ignore suspicious activity. Photograph: Manuel Breva Colmeiro/Getty Images 
The FBI has accused those websites of deliberately obscuring their true location to deceive applicants. It told a US court the website impersonating Horizzen has been registered in India. 
“While we cannot comment on an ongoing investigation, the FBI is aware that malicious online actors often use ‘spoofing’ or other techniques to appear legitimate when targeting innocent people and businesses,” an FBI spokesperson told Guardian Australia. 
The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation did not comment on Horizzen’s experience, but has repeatedly warned of similar espionage activity. 
In 2024, Asio alleged a spy ring known as “the A team” was targeting Australians with access to privileged information on LinkedIn. 
“The spies pose as consultants, headhunters, local government officials, academics and thinktank researchers, claiming to be from fictional companies,” Asio’s annual threat assessment said. 
‘Frightening scale’
While the suspicious emails and calls to Horizzen’s team have stopped, they remain concerned their experience may be increasingly common. 
Like the FBI, they worry that rapid developments in artificial intelligence are making it easier for malicious actors to deceive innocent people. 
“My experience shows that online impersonation can be far more serious than it first appears,” the spokesperson said. 
“Whether or not AI was used in this case, AI gives opportunists the ability to create convincing websites, communications, images and corporate identities quickly, cheaply and at frightening scale.” 
Five Eyes intelligence agencies are urging anyone who believes they have communicated with a suspicious consultancy firm or recruiter to report all details of their interaction. 
“Ensure you disengage from the profile and don’t interact any further,” Asio’s official guidance says. 
In Brisbane, Horizzen is urging people not to ignore any suspicious activity. 
“Businesses and individuals need to take unexpected approaches, strange websites and apparent impersonation seriously, because what looks like ordinary spam may be connected to something far more sinister,” the spokesperson says.

View image in fullscreen 
The average number of people travelling on each Channel-crossing dinghy has sharply increased in recent years. Photograph: SNMS Berck sur Mer/AFP/Getty Images 
How to buy a ‘mega-dinghy’: the perilous new model of Channel crossing
Boats carrying hundreds of people are a clear and alarming trend. But where do such large vessels come from? 
P roviding a large dinghy for use in the choppy seas of western Europe was not a problem, as long as the order was for more than 20 vessels, they said. The sales manager at the Chinese company even had an online brochure for an undercover Guardian reporter, posing as a prospective client, to peruse. 
They had a production capacity of 500 boats a month and, yes, it was possible to get even bigger ones for the right price. They could do a seven or even an eight-metre military-style dinghy for $1,678 (£1,238) a boat, without the engines, but that would be lacking CE certification, the mandatory mark that shows a product meets EU health and safety requirements. 
“We can sell this big boat to China warehouse only,” wrote the sales manager on the Made in China messaging platform. From there, it was up to the client to export it and get the right certification. 
In the early hours of Monday morning, a full-to-the-brim dinghy of a type similar to that being offered by the Chinese salesperson arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel with a record 230 people onboard . French authorities say there have been 11 such “mega-dinghy” crossings of the Channel so far this year. Last week one of those carrying 173 people capsized after its engine caught fire. 
It is a clear and perilous trend. An analysis by the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, based on Home Office figures, shows how the number of people travelling on a dinghy has sharply increased since the crossings first began nearly a decade ago. 
In 2018, there would be an average of seven people per small boat. That ticked up to 13 by 2020. The number shifted up to 27 by the following year and by 2022 it was 41. The average number of people on a dinghy crossing is up to 66.5 people in the first six months of 2026. These are often no longer small boats. The length of the dinghy that arrived this week was 15 metres. Graph: average number of people per dinghy each year since 2018 
Where are the “mega-dinghies” coming from? The sales manager offering boats to an undercover Guardian reporter worked for a company called Wuxi Funsor Marine Equipment that is described on its own website as a subsidiary of the Weihai Yamar Outdoors Product Co Ltd. 
Weihai Yamar, which is headquartered in an industrial park in Wenquan Town in Weihai, in the eastern Chinese province of Shandong, was put under economic sanctions by the UK in July last year for offering rigid inflatable boats for sale on online retail platforms to organised crime gangs smuggling people across the Channel. Weihai’s largest shareholder at the time is now the main shareholder of Wuxi Funsor Marine Equipment. Weihai Yamar has denied advertising lifeboats and boats for migrants online. 
The likely onward journey of dinghies from eastern China can be traced thanks to the recent trial of Adem Savas, a Turkish national identified by the National Crime Agency (NCA) as one of the key enablers of small boat crossings . 
Between 2019 and 2024, Savas was said by the NCA to have supplied inflatable boats, outboard engines and equipment to gangs across Europe, enabling thousands of crossings, including around half of all Channel crossings in 2023, generating millions of pounds in profit. 
Savas was the primary equipment supplier to a Kurdish smuggler, Hewa Rahimpur . 
The boats and engines were sourced largely from China, transported from Turkey through Bulgaria, and stored in Germany before onward distribution to smuggling networks in Belgium and France. 
A Netherlands-based haulage firm facilitated the logistics. A raid coordinated by Europol in December 2024 resulted in 25 searches in Germany and the seizure of equipment and cash. 
Savas pleaded guilty in a court in Bruges to people-smuggling and being a member of an organised crime group and was sentenced to 11 years’ imprisonment and a €400,000 (£340,000) fine. Savas’s co-defendants received combined sentences of 38 years. 
A spokesperson for Europol said the shift to larger boats was plausibly an indication that the gangs were getting desperate. 
“I can confirm that Europol – and within our agency specifically the experts forming the European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling (ECAMS) – is aware of this development,” the spokesperson said. 
“We are in constant exchange with the appropriate authorities in both France and the United Kingdom on this phenomenon and also have a dedicated operational taskforce running that concentrates on smuggling of migrants with boats (no matter if relatively small boats or, as of recently, larger boats) across the Channel. 
“As with any criminal phenomenon, a change of tactics used by criminal networks may be the result of law enforcement pressure.” 
Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory, said the mega-dinghy phenomenon made economic sense for the gangs as they faced pressures on their supply chains from the authorities. 
“It’s simply much more efficient, much more profitable for gangs to pack as many people as possible on one boat,” he said. “What we’ve seen in the last few weeks with some of these so-called mega-dinghies is an acceleration of this longstanding trend. 
“It’s very likely to do with increased enforcement in and around the French coast in particular. We’ve seen the authorities work, quite differently, targeting the supply chains and making it hard to get hold of the small boats in the first place.” 
Weihai Yamar did not respond to a request for comment.

Despite the recent hearings in Congress, we seem to be even further from the goal of understanding Covid-19’s origin’s than we have ever been 
A s a microbiologist and infectious disease clinician, it has been tough to watch the recent devolution of public discourse on Covid-19 origins. It has been especially difficult for me to read the comments of Anthony Fauci about the origins debate in his now-public diary . And it has been painful to watch the televised spectacle hosted by the US senator Rand Paul on 29 July involving a hostile interrogation of Fauci. 
Despite many early pleas, including my own , for a dispassionate, objective assessment of what we know, don’t know and need to know about Covid-19 origins, we seem to be even further from this goal now than we have ever been – plagued by politicization, polarization and illogical thinking. 
Much is at stake: trust in science, scientists and government, not to mention our ability to thwart and respond to the next pandemic. How did this happen and how do we dig ourselves out? Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty | Margaret Sullivan 
Read more 
By the eve of Covid-19, after 20 years of debate, we had agreed to disagree about whether humans were capable of starting a new pandemic. Most public health scientists believed that nature was the only important “bioterrorist” , based simply on prior probabilities. 
Other scientists, who focused on the growing power of biotechnology and studied human behavior, believed that humans had become more than fully capable . When Covid suddenly blew up in late December 2019 in Wuhan, China, and was quickly attributed to a coronavirus with recent ancestors in bats, two possibilities leaped to the fore: a natural “spillover” at one of the unregulated wildlife markets in the city (as with the original 2002 Sars outbreak), and a lab accident in Wuhan, where there happened to be the world’s largest collection of bat-associated coronaviruses. 
Six years later, despite much mudslinging, each of these possibilities remains viable, supported by circumstantial, but not dispositive, evidence. The virus has not been found in nature, nor in a lab. 
At the heart of the dispute, two statements are true but not necessarily related. First, we see in scientific publications that risky work with bat coronaviruses was undertaken in Wuhan, some with US National Institutes of Health (NIH) support. 
Its goal was prediction of disease emergence. Some of this work resembled a form of Russian roulette, in which pieces of novel bat viruses were shuffled to make chimeric viruses and then test their properties (under inadequate biosafety conditions). 
Yet, this published work does not reveal a plausible Covid precursor virus. Thus, Rand Paul is correct in that risky work was funded by NIH in Wuhan. Anthony Fauci is correct in that the published work, on the face of it, did not cause Covid. Of course, as with any research program, we can assume that much remains unpublished. 
My own view, for what it is worth, is that a lab accident in Wuhan is the most plausible explanation for Covid, given the kind of work pursued there, the fact that publications by Chinese researchers indicate knowledge about the Sars-CoV-2 virus before late December 2019, and the thousands of negative tests from suspect animal reservoirs. But I could be wrong. 
If we are to improve our capacity for anticipating, preventing and responding to the next pandemic, several things must happen. First, everyone who insists that they know how Covid began should back off, accept ongoing uncertainty and display a bit more humility. 
Second, we need an objective and transparent forensic investigation of Covid origins with broad international engagement and proper authorities and accountability. 
Third, scientists must fully embrace the responsibilities that come with technical power and knowledge and accept guardrails for some kinds of experiments. Similarly, political representatives must embrace their responsibilities for ensuring an educated, balanced public discussion about the trade-offs between a healthy pursuit of public health science and the attendant risks, as well as for balanced public policy addressing risk oversight. 
One thing that cannot continue to happen is a collective state of wishful thinking that this issue can be ignored or buried, or that nothing useful will result from addressing it. Continuing down the current path comes at our own peril.

David Relman is a professor of medicine and microbiology at Stanford University. He was an inaugural member of the US National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity and president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

Taiwan practised cutting off internet for the first time amid concerns about the safety of the undersea cables that form its ‘digital lifeline’ 
In Taipei, the streets swiftly empty as air raid sirens ring out and alerts ping on mobile phones. Police officers usher any stragglers into shelters, leaving the capital suddenly deserted. 
In cities across Taiwan, these kinds of drills are a fact of life every year , amid the growing threat posed by China across the strait, but this time there is something different. 
Internet speeds were drastically cut on Thursday, simulating a coordinated attack for the first time. Data-heavy services such as video calls, streaming and mobile payments became difficult or impossible to use, while videos on social media barely loaded. 
However, Wang Chen-wen knows how to reach others. 
When the sirens sound and her mobile internet begins to grind to a halt, Wang goes to the roof of her 25-storey apartment building, searching for a better radio signal. She connects her phone via Bluetooth to a small, flat device hanging from her bag. Within seconds, she is sending messages without relying on the internet. Minutes later, some of them succeeded in reaching a friend in a neighbouring district. 
View image in fullscreen 
People take shelter inside metro stations, during an air raid drill in Taipei. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images 
View image in fullscreen 
Photograph: Cheng Yu-Chen/AFP/Getty Images 
“Testing from Beitou district, Taipei.” “Xinyi district, Taipei.” Messages begin coming in as users share their locations in a group chat being tested on an open-source platform that allows people to use text messages via long-range, low-power radio signals. 
“You can’t wait until something actually happens to realise you should have prepared,” says Wang, who leads a local group that provides civil defence training and started learning how to use the platform about six months ago. 
Authorities said the drill was designed to encourage people to prepare alternative means of communication in an emergency – part of Taiwan’s efforts to strengthen its civil resilience in the face of growing military threats from Beijing, which claims the self-ruling democracy as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to annex it. 
Taiwan's simulated internet blackout, explained – video 
The internet disruption exercise took place on two separate days this week across 14 cities and counties in northern and central Taiwan , home to roughly 70% of the island’s 23 million people. 
“If the idea is to recreate what it might be like during a war, it’s definitely inconvenient, but I can understand why they’re doing it,” says Jimmy Chu, a 22-year-old worker who says messages from his boss failed to come through during the drill. 
Tzeng Yi-suo, an associate researcher at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, says the inconvenience itself was intentional. 
View image in fullscreen 
An open-source platform was tested that allows people to send and receive text messages via long-range, low-power radio signals. Photograph: Yu-chen Li/The Guardian 
“It’s a starting point for raising public awareness,” Tzeng says. “Through repeated exercises, people will gradually understand that this is about experiencing that inconvenience and testing the backup systems we may need.” 
For Chen Hui-xuan, an 18-year-old who tried to use her phone on the metro during the drill, the inconvenience was real. “TikTok wouldn’t open at all. Facebook worked, but it was really slow, and messages on Instagram took around 30 seconds to send,” she says. 
There is growing concern about the vulnerability of Taiwan’s submarine cable network – 16 international cables and 10 domestic ones – which the government has called an “irreplaceable digital lifeline”. 
View image in fullscreen 
Several undersea cables have been damaged in recent years in incidents involving Chinese or China-linked vessels. Photograph: Cheng Yu-Chen/AFP/Getty Images 
Several cables have been damaged in recent years in incidents involving Chinese or China-linked vessels, which Taiwan’s coast guard has described as a “grey zone” strategy aimed at depleting the island’s resources without crossing the threshold into an act of war. 
In 2025, a Chinese captain was convicted of deliberately damaging a cable linking Taiwan’s main island with the offshore Penghu archipelago, while another Chinese fishing boat captain was later convicted of negligently damaging a cable serving Matsu, another outlying archipelago administered by Taiwan. Taiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attack 
Read more 
Taiwan is seeking to build multiple layers of backup communications so that no single disruption can cut off the island. The options include low-Earth-orbit satellite services that could help people stay connected should terrestrial networks be disrupted. 
The approach has drawn on lessons learned in Ukraine, where Elon Musk’s Starlink has played a role after conventional infrastructure was damaged during Russia’s invasion. Last month, Taiwan’s legislature approved amendments that could clear the way for Starlink to enter the local market, although relying on Musk’s network has raised concerns because of his extensive business interests in China. 
In a crisis where internet access was limited, Tzeng says people would face “a high degree of uncertainty and fear”, which hostile forces could exploit. “The question is how you use the backup communications channels available to get reliable information to people and reassure them.” 
For Wang, knowing she has another way to communicate has already made a difference. “At least I know that if something happens, I already have a basic plan and know what to do, so I won’t face whatever disaster may come with fear or panic,” she says.

Meaningful diplomacy on an international level is well overdue, writes Jennifer Hubbard . Plus letters from Geoffrey Dixon and Jane Renton 
In his article on China’s latest tool for suppression of minorities, the “ethnic unity” law, Simon Tisdall seems to take it as read that western governments will continue to pay lip service to notions of human rights in China while pursuing short-term economic goals, ultimately destructive to their own productivity ( President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip, 8 August ). 
This has been the pattern since June 1989, the Tiananmen Square massacre. His faint hope that the young urban Chinese might overturn Xi’s regime is a judgment on the failure of western governments to show any foresight, integrity, effective diplomacy, joined-up thinking or action. They rely on the self-sacrifice of individuals such as Jimmy Lai , Lobga Rangzen and countless – often to us nameless – individuals who put their lives on the line while we wring our hands and weep crocodile tears. 
Their response to this latest abuse of power seems to be limited to a change in their extradition policy to protect their own citizens. They should understand by now that the law alone will not protect critics of Xi’s regime, wherever they are. Meaningful diplomacy on an international level is well overdue, but just as Europe has had to wean itself off dependence on the US for defence, so it will need to wean itself off China for trade.
Jennifer Hubbard 
Burton-in-Kendal, Cumbria 
Very striking is what Simon Tisdall’s article concedes and then ignores. It notes in passing an American administration displaying “disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland)”, tariff wars against allies, and partners who now have to regard Washington as unreliable. Every charge laid against Beijing’s ambitions applies to conduct the article treats as merely regrettable background. 
Tisdall asks us to imagine a British prime minister banning the Welsh language from schools. It is an unfortunate choice. Britain did precisely that – the Welsh Not was an instrument of state policy, Gaelic was suppressed, and Irish self-determination was resisted by force for centuries. 
The analogy does not illuminate China’s conduct so much as remind us that the moral vantage point being claimed is a recent acquisition. 
The repression in Xinjiang and Tibet is real and deserves condemnation. But condemnation is weakened, not strengthened, when it is deployed selectively as an instrument of strategic competition. Britain’s silence is not the “debilitating fatalism” Tisdall diagnoses; it is the ordinary conduct of a state that raises human rights with rivals and sets them aside with customers. Further, quoting a statement from a US admiral without criticism – from a rogue nation engaged in economic and political warfare against China – shows a bias I did not expect to find.
Geoffrey Dixon 
Burston, Norfolk 
Simon Tisdall writes “imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament”. We don’t have to imagine – it happened in 1979. In the referendum that year, a majority of those voting said yes to a Scottish parliament. But because of the Cunningham amendment from an MP representing Islington in London, which required 40% of the electorate to vote yes, we had to wait another 20 years for our parliament. Had this rule been applied in the Brexit referendum, we would still be in the EU. Val McDermid writes about this in her novel 1979. 
Jane Renton 
Edinburgh
